newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - S.Africa and old foes haggle over free-trade zone.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - S.Africa and old foes haggle over free-trade zone.

text.p: Southern African countries all agree that prosperity lies in a regional free trade zone, but the problems of the past are haunting them as they try to achieve it.

They must not only merge South Africa's relative might with the economic minnows around it, but also fuse a five-nation customs union that served the apartheid state with the old alliance of "Frontline" states set up to oppose it.

A workshop in Cape Town this month of members of parliament from the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC) made clear the sharp differences of opinion that still exist between them on the way forward.

The most contentious issues were the link between the trade protocol of SADC, the group set up to help black-ruled states lessen economic dependence on South Africa in the anti-apartheid struggle, and the renegotiation of the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), whose five members now all belong to SADC too.

SACU, made up of South Africa and its immediate neighbours, Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Swaziland, dates back to the turn of the century and lasted through four decades of racial segregation in South Africa and into the post-apartheid era.
It provides a common external tariff and customs-revenue sharing, a form of economic integration far deeper than anything SADC yet envisages.
The SACU agreement is now being re-negotiated with South Africa's weaker neighbours demanding a greater say in setting tariffs than the minority white regime ever allowed them.
FRIENDS AND FORMER FOES
The SADC, whose other members are Angola, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Tanzania and the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius, is also planning a great leap forward.
Heads of state agreed last September to work towards a regional free trade area by 2004 and the nitty gritty negotiation of tariff reduction schedules now has to begin.
The two largest economies, South Africa and Zimbabwe, are still fiercely fighting their corners in protracted bilateral trade liberalisation talks.

Their slow progress does not bode well for multilateral talks to make a regional market of 140 million people in eight years -- a period many businessmen say is too slow but which governments say is needed to iron out the vast differences in relative strengths and employment problems in the region.
Some states have criticsed South Africa for declining to ratify the SADC free trade protocol until tariff reductions have been hammered out.

South Africa trade ministry assistant director John Kodisang raised the hackles of several delegates at the workshop when he said Pretoria wanted more concrete details of what would be involved before it would ratify the protocol.
NO BLANK CHEQUE
"There is no way that we are going to sign a blank cheque. There are quite a number of issues that have to be clarified, including rules of origin," he said.
The protocol will become binding on all member states only once it has been ratified by two thirds of them. From that date, the aim is to phase in a free trade area within eight years.
So far, only Mauritius and Tanzania have ratified it.
Kodisang said South Africa's initial tariff reduction offer would be on the table by November, but other SADC states had given no indication yet of when they would be ready.
Resentment also brewed among some non-SACU parliamentarians, such as those from Mauritius and Zimbabwe, who wanted SACU to be done away with.
A Zambian member proposed that other states should follow Lusaka's example of sharply cutting all tariffs.
"This has caused untold difficulties for Zambia, but it will be easier if we all do it," said Vernon Waanga, chairman of Zambia's foreign affairs committee.
Rob Davies, chairman of South Africa's parliamentary trade and industry committee, disagreed, saying Zambia had cut tariffs towards the world at large and not towards the region only.
"They are now saying they have done the right thing. But that is not the real issue. What you do at a regional level may be different to what you do towards the world outside," he said.
"You don't necessarily want to go to rock bottom to the world outside where there is an unequal process of liberalisation with the European Union, for example, giving subsidies to exporters."

SADC members, like other African Caribbean Pacific (ACP) countries whose trade terms with the European Union are defined in the Lome Convention, fear the consequences of a free trade area which South Africa is about to start negotiating with the EU.
The current Lome Convention will expire in 1999 and there are very real fears that its successor will be less generous to ACP states.
